result: The authors demonstrate that preferences are not fixed during a single experimental session. Participants were more likely to select the same option when presentations of the same pair were closer in time, with a highly significant negative regression coefficient (p<0.0001) for the number of trials between repetitions.
evaluation: All three reviewers affirm the core finding that subjective values change across sequences of decisions. The editor states the authors 'provide convincing evidence that the subjective values human participants assign to items change across sequences of multiple decisions,' and reviewers explicitly note the authors 'clearly demonstrate this re-evaluation phenomenon in several existing datasets.'

result: The Reval algorithm produces dynamic values (d-values) that explain choices and response times better than static values (s-values). The DDM using d-values provided better fits for all participants, explained more variance in RT, and better classified easy vs. difficult trials.
evaluation: Reviewers explicitly affirm that 'estimations of dynamic valuation correlate with neural activity' and that the evidence is 'solid.' One reviewer states 'food choice outcomes and BOLD signal in the vmPFC are better explained by algorithms that update subjective values during the sequence of choices compared to algorithms based on static values.' The methods are described as 'novel' and 'robust.'

result: Control analyses demonstrate that improvements from Reval are not artifacts. The reduction in deviance was negligible in simulated data, variance explained was greater when Reval was applied in the correct temporal order (p<0.0001), and even backward Reval explained choices better than static values.
evaluation: Reviewers explicitly note that 'the authors provided evidence for the behaviour effect using several techniques and generated surrogate data (where the ground truth is known) to demonstrate the robustness of their methods.' The control analyses are treated as convincing validation of the main findings.

result: fMRI analysis revealed that vmPFC BOLD signal significantly correlated with d-values (controlling for s-values), and d-values alone showed robust effects surviving whole-brain correction, while s-values alone did not survive correction.
evaluation: Reviewers explicitly state that 'estimations of dynamic valuation correlate with neural activity in prefrontal cortex' and that 'BOLD signal in the vmPFC are better explained by algorithms that update subjective values.' The neural evidence is treated as supporting the behavioral findings without critique.

result: Reval was applied to three independent datasets with largely similar results. The reduction in deviance was significantly greater than simulated data in all datasets. Forward vs. backward Reval showed significant differences in Folke et al. (2016) but not in Sepulveda et al. (2020).
evaluation: Reviewers note the authors 'clearly demonstrate this re-evaluation phenomenon in several existing datasets,' treating the replication as evidence of robustness. The mixed result in one dataset (C33) is acknowledged by the authors as potentially due to experimental design idiosyncrasies (C91), and reviewers do not challenge this interpretation.

result: A novel correlated-evidence drift-diffusion model (ceDDM) with temporally correlated evidence samples reproduces key behavioral patterns. The model shows correlation of 0.1062±0.0113 after 1s, and when Reval is applied to ceDDM simulations, it increases RT range by difficulty, explains choices better in forward than backward direction, and mirrors patterns in real data.
evaluation: Reviewers describe the ceDDM as a 'novel' contribution and note the authors 'generated surrogate data (where the ground truth is known) to demonstrate the robustness of their methods.' The modeling work is treated as supporting the interpretation that revaluation reflects dynamic value construction during deliberation.

result: For most participants, revaluation is greater for chosen than unchosen items, which is consistent with chosen items being attended longer and the ceDDM prediction that correlation decreases with evidence sampling.
evaluation: Reviewers do not challenge this asymmetric revaluation finding. It is presented as consistent with established attention patterns and model predictions, and reviewers affirm the overall evidence as 'solid' without raising concerns about this specific result.

result: The sequential effects can be interpreted as choice-induced preference change (CIPC), cannot be explained by the Chen and Risen (2010) artifact, and the approach does not require pre- and post-choice ratings but instead requires repeated item presentations.
evaluation: Reviewers explicitly state 'there is a long-standing idea that choices influence evaluation' and affirm the authors 'clearly demonstrate this re-evaluation phenomenon.' The methodological advantages and distinction from prior artifacts are not questioned by reviewers.

result: Participants chose the higher s-value item in only 64% of trials, showing behavior similar to other studies. A regression model using choices from other trials is superior to s-values for predicting choices, demonstrating that explicit value reports have limited predictive power.
evaluation: Reviewers do not question these basic behavioral observations. They are treated as establishing the context for the main findings about dynamic values. The comparison to prior studies and the limited predictive power of static values are accepted without critique.

result: The authors acknowledge several limitations: the study only examined food items with explicit value reports, other elicitation methods remain to be tested, perceptual decisions may show similar patterns, the Sepulveda dataset failure may relate to experimental design, and alternative stochastic processes might explain the observations.
evaluation: Reviewers explicitly praise the authors for 'avoid[ing] over-selling the work, with a lucid description of limitations, and potential for further exploration of the work, in the discussion.' The acknowledgment of limitations is treated as a strength rather than undermining the main findings. One reviewer notes the evidence is 'currently limited to choices between food items because no other goods were examined.'

result: The study re-examined data from Bakkour et al. (2019) with 30 participants who rated 60 snack items ($0-$3) and completed 210 trials with each item appearing seven times. The experimental procedures included rating revision opportunities, specific trial timing (500ms confirmation, exponential ITI distribution with mean 3.05s), and IRB approval.
evaluation: Reviewers do not question the methodological details or experimental design. The reanalysis of existing data is accepted, and reviewers note the methods are 'well-written' with 'clear' figures. The experimental procedures are treated as appropriate for addressing the research questions.
